title: Final review week
intro: Use this plan in the last 7 days before you sit the CSOE, once you have studied SOXCPA's presentations and worked through the topics. The aim now is to sharpen recall and pace for an open-book, forward-only exam, not to learn new material. Most days take about an hour.
how_it_works: You choose when to sit the CSOE, so pick your exam day first and count back seven days.
Short reviews spread over several days hold up better than one long session the night before.
Answer from memory first, then check. Recalling builds memory; rereading mostly makes pages feel familiar, and recall is what saves time on an open-book exam.
Memory settles while you sleep, so a full night's rest is part of the plan, not a break from it.
Missed a day? Skip it and carry on with today's plan. Doubling up turns review into cramming.
SOXCPA includes up to three attempts a year. Prepare for the first one, and let that fact ease the pressure, not the preparation.

days.title: Full timed rehearsal
days.goal: Sit one full timed mock and hold yourself to the real exam's rules, to test your pace, your lookups and your focus.

tasks.text: Take a full timed KaiSip mock in one sitting: 35 questions in 90 minutes. Answer in order and never go back, even if the screen allows it.
Keep the open-book habit: answer from memory first, and look up only one exact number or date when you must.
A KaiSip mock score is not a SOXCPA score. Your misses go to your mistake journal; rest tonight and review them tomorrow.

days.remember: One mock is a rehearsal, not a verdict. On a short exam, a score can swing from one sitting to the next.

days.title: Learn from every miss
days.goal: Trace each mock miss to the rule or the slip behind it, starting with the heaviest domains. Stop after about 90 minutes.

tasks.text: In your mistake journal, review yesterday's mock misses, starting with Domains 4 and 5, the heaviest in KaiSip's estimate.
Tag why you missed each one: “Acted as the wrong person”, “Missed FIRST or BEST”, “Tool before policy”, “Fixed the symptom, not the cause”, “Misread” or “Didn’t know it”.
On CSOE items, read the tags this way: wrong person means wrong actor; tool before policy means good practice over the rule; symptom means judging by the error found.
Read the principles behind the slip you tagged most.
From memory, list three Domain 4 and three Domain 5 points. Then open the lists and check.

days.remember: A miss you understand is worth more than a right answer you guessed.

days.title: Your biggest gap
days.goal: Work on the domain where your readiness is furthest behind its weight, recalling each rule before you check it.

tasks.text: Before opening your focus domain's list, write down what you remember. Then check for gaps.
Answer a short set in that domain from memory, without opening your materials, and read every explanation.
For a rule you missed more than once, read its note, then close it and say the section, who acts, what, by when and the consequence.
Read the principles on who must act: management owns, the auditor attests, and the SEC oversees the PCAOB.
Read the principles on consequences: civil or criminal, penalty tiers, and disclose or explain.

days.remember: On CSOE items, the actor and the section usually decide the answer before any detail does.

days.title: Pace check
days.goal: Keep your forward-only pace sharp with one timed mini mock, and refresh scope and severity.

tasks.text: Take a timed mini mock in one sitting and answer in order without going back. Watch your pace more than the score.
From memory, list three Domain 1 and three Domain 2 points. Then open the lists and check.
Without looking, say how Rule 12b-2 sorts filers and which filers skip the auditor's attestation. Then check the note.
Read the principles on scope: filer status and dates, who is covered, and scope following the reporting risk.
Read the principles on control severity: reasonable possibility, and the year-end conclusion.

days.remember: This is your last timed test before the exam. From here on, short recall keeps you sharp.

days.title: Read like the exam
days.goal: Sharpen how you read each question, cover Domain 3, and work on your second gap without a timer.

tasks.text: From memory, list three Domain 3 points, including what separates Sections 302, 404 and 906. Then open the list and check.
Say the answering steps and the seven priority words from memory, then check them.
Read the principles on reading the question, including incomplete statements and open book but fast.
Practice a short untimed set in your second-weakest domain. Before you choose, name the actor and the rule.
Redo your mistake journal questions. Before you choose, say which detail makes your old answer lose.

days.remember: Several options can be true somewhere in the law. Only one fits the actor, the section and the date in the question.

days.title: Light review and setup
days.goal: Recall everything once, lightly, and set up your materials and exam access so nothing on the day is a surprise.

tasks.text: For each domain, recall two points before you open its list. Spend a few minutes, not an hour.
Read the principles on the rule itself: the rule decides, find the section, and the law as amended.
Look up any term on the lists that still feels fuzzy.
Set up your open-book materials: bookmark the presentations and finish a one-page list of deadlines, thresholds and penalties, each with its section.
Check that you have your exam username and password from SOXCPA, and plan a quiet 90 minutes with a reliable connection.

days.remember: Recall beats rereading. Leave new material alone now.

days.title: The eve
days.goal: Stay fresh, not tired: a light touch early in the day, then rest.

tasks.text: Optional: answer up to 10 mistake journal questions, then stop. A miss today is a reminder, not a warning.
Read the reminder for the slip you make most often.
Read the pace lines once, so the forward-only rhythm feels familiar tomorrow.
Work through the eve checklist.
Close the books by early evening and keep your usual bedtime.

days.remember: Rest is part of the plan. If sleep comes slowly tonight, that is common, and your preparation is already done.

eve: You have the exam username, password and account details that SOXCPA emailed you, and you know where to sign in.
You have a quiet place and 90 free minutes with no interruptions, plus a reliable internet connection.
Your device is charged or plugged in, with updates done, so it will not restart mid-exam. Closing the browser ends the attempt.
Your study PDFs are bookmarked, and your one-page list of deadlines, thresholds and penalties is ready.
You have read the reminder for your most common slip.
If worries keep circling, write them down for a few minutes, then put the page away.
Books are closed by early evening, and you keep your usual bedtime.
morning: Eat a familiar breakfast and keep your usual caffeine.
Reread your pace plan: about 2.5 minutes a question, forward only, recall first and look up only one exact fact.
Before you start, read the exam terms on screen: the time limit, the back button, restarting and skipping.
Silence notifications and close other programs, so nothing pulls you out of the exam window.
A racing heart is your body getting ready. Treat it as energy for focus, not a sign of danger.
If your mind goes blank, breathe out slowly, cross out the options you know are wrong, and choose the best of the rest.

domains.name: Scope and reach of the Act

points.text: An issuer has securities registered under Exchange Act Section 12, must report under Section 15(d), or has a Securities Act registration statement filed and not yet effective or withdrawn.

Rule 12b-2 sorts filers by public float, reporting history and a revenue test: accelerated from $75 million of float, large accelerated from $700 million. Revenues under $100 million with float under $700 million keep an issuer non-accelerated.

Management's Section 404(a) report applies to every reporting issuer (registered funds aside) after its first annual report. The auditor's 404(b) attestation skips non-accelerated filers and emerging growth companies.
Registered investment companies are outside Sections 401, 402 and 404 (Section 405). Crimes written for anyone, such as Section 1519, reach private companies' staff too.
Annual report deadlines: 60 days for large accelerated, 75 for accelerated and 90 for non-accelerated filers. Quarterly reports: 40 or 45 days.
Foreign private issuers file Form 20-F within 4 months of year-end and furnish Form 6-K in between. The officers certify the 20-F, not a 6-K.
ADR levels: Level 1 trades over the counter with no periodic reports to certify; Level 2 adds an exchange listing and Form 20-F; only Level 3 raises new capital.
The PCAOB is a nonprofit corporation, not a federal agency: five full-time members, two and only two of them current or former CPAs, appointed by the SEC.
Board rules and standards take effect only after SEC approval, and the SEC can review Board sanctions. Issuers, and since 2010 brokers and dealers, fund the Board through accounting support fees.
No registration, no issuer audit (Section 102). A firm with more than 100 issuer clients is inspected every year; others at least every three years.

Nine non-audit services are banned for the issuer's auditor, and preapproval cannot cure them. Permitted services need the audit committee's advance approval, delegable only to its independent members, with a narrow de minimis exception.
Lead and reviewing partners rotate after five consecutive years. Title II rotates partners, not firms; Section 207 only ordered a study of firm rotation.
The auditor reports critical accounting policies, alternative treatments discussed with management and its own preference to the audit committee, not to the CFO (Section 204).
Cooling off: a firm cannot audit an issuer whose CEO, CFO, controller or chief accounting officer worked on that issuer's audit at the firm in the year before the audit began.
The audit committee appoints, pays and oversees the auditor, resolves auditor-management disputes and sets complaint procedures, including anonymous employee submissions (Section 301).
Section 302: the CEO and CFO certify each annual and quarterly report, covering accuracy, fair presentation, controls, and disclosures to the auditor and audit committee. It is civil.
Section 906: criminal certification of compliance and fair presentation. Knowing: up to $1 million and 10 years. Willful: up to $5 million and 20 years.
Section 404(a): management's annual report on internal control, as of fiscal year-end, naming its framework. A material weakness open at year-end means not effective, with no except-for wording.
A material weakness is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement is not prevented or detected on time, whether or not an error occurred.
Section 304: after a restatement caused by misconduct, the CEO and CFO repay bonuses, other incentive- or equity-based pay and stock-sale profits from the 12 months after the misstated filing.

Sections 406 and 407 are disclose-or-explain, and code waivers for senior financial officers are disclosed immediately (Form 8-K or online, within four business days). Section 403: insider trades are reported by the end of the second business day.
The 1933 Act registers new offerings; the 1934 Act created the SEC and governs trading and periodic reports. A SOX violation is treated as an Exchange Act violation.
SEC tools are civil: inquiries, formal orders with subpoenas, Wells notices, actions and settlements. Criminal charges belong to the Justice Department, and no SEC settlement covers them.
Section 1519: anyone who destroys or falsifies records to obstruct a federal matter, pending or expected, faces up to 20 years. Section 1520 covers auditors' workpapers.

Section 806 protects public company employees, including those of consolidated subsidiaries, who report fraud. They file with the Secretary of Labor within 180 days, and predispute arbitration agreements do not apply.
Dodd-Frank awards: original information given voluntarily to the SEC that leads to sanctions over $1 million earns 10 to 30 percent, paid from the Investor Protection Fund.
Title IX: attempts and conspiracies carry the completed offense's penalty, and mail and wire fraud rose to 20 years.
Dodd-Frank added Section 404(c), exempting non-accelerated filers from the auditor's attestation; management's 404(a) report still applies.

domains.name: Internal control frameworks and SOX scope

points.text: Internal control is a process run by people that gives reasonable, not absolute, assurance on operations, reporting and compliance objectives.
SEC rules require a suitable, recognized framework, not COSO by name, and management's report must identify the framework it used.
COSO 2013 kept the five components and set out 17 principles; it replaced the 1992 edition after 15 December 2014.
Effective means each relevant principle is present and functioning and the components operate together. SEC filers still rate deficiencies in the SEC's terms.
ERM 2017 has five components and 20 principles and ties risk to strategy. ERM is broader than internal control, and neither framework supersedes the other.
Scope follows the reporting risk: spreadsheets and systems behind key controls are in scope, and only the IT general controls those controls depend on are evaluated.
Outsourcing keeps the responsibility with management. A SOC 1 Type 2 report shows controls operated over a period; a Type 1 speaks only as of a date.

principles.intro: The CSOE mindset principles, one line each. Read a few a day this week, starting with the family behind your most common slip.

priority_words.meaning: Order. Which step must happen before the others, such as registering with the PCAOB before any issuer audit work, or audit committee approval before a service starts.
priority_words.cue: Ask: what must the rule see happen first?

priority_words.meaning: SOXCPA's own instruction is to look for the best answer, not just a correct one. The best option fits the rule's actor, timing and scope exactly.
priority_words.cue: Ask: which option fits every fact given?

priority_words.meaning: A ranking on one named quality, such as MOST accurate or MOST directly. On rule questions, MOST directly usually points to the specific section, not a general one.
priority_words.cue: Ask: most what, and under which section?

priority_words.meaning: The main responsibility or purpose the rule assigns, not a side role. Management has the primary duty for internal control; others support or oversee it.
priority_words.cue: Ask: whom does the rule hold responsible?

priority_words.meaning: The largest amount the text allows, such as a statutory maximum penalty or the longest interval permitted. Find the exact tier before picking the biggest number.
priority_words.cue: Ask: greatest under which tier or section?

priority_words.meaning: Probability, not severity. Pick the outcome that best fits all the facts given, even if another would be worse.
priority_words.cue: Ask: which outcome do the rule and these facts point to?

priority_words.meaning: Flip the logic. Three options fit the rule; find the one that fits least or not at all.
priority_words.cue: Ask: which one does the rule not support?

answering_routine.title: Read the last line first
answering_routine.text: Is it a direct question or an incomplete statement? Note exactly what completes it: an actor, a section, a date, a number or a consequence.

answering_routine.title: Find the actor and the rule
answering_routine.text: Who acts in the facts, and which section or rule governs them? Check filer status and dates when the answer depends on them.

answering_routine.title: Note any priority word
answering_routine.text: If the question says FIRST, BEST, MOST or GREATEST, hold it in mind. If it names a section, ask directly what that section requires.

answering_routine.title: Eliminate two
answering_routine.text: Cross out options with the wrong actor, the wrong section, a superseded rule, or good practice the rule does not demand.

answering_routine.title: Decide between the final two
answering_routine.text: Name the one exact point that splits them: actor, timing, threshold, civil or criminal, or scope. Then answer; you cannot come back.

pace: 90 minutes for 35 questions is about 2.5 minutes each. Aim for about 2 minutes to keep time for a few lookups.
Checkpoints: around question 15 at 30 minutes and question 30 at 60 minutes.
Forward only: no going back, no skipping and no pause. Every answer is final when you give it.
Open book is a backup: recall first, and look up only one exact number or date.
Running past 90 minutes, or closing the browser, counts as an unsuccessful attempt.
